<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:certification}
Let $\pi$ have a density on $\mathbb R^d$, and let $k$ be a bounded characteristic kernel with RKHS $\mathcal H$. Let the checklist $v_1,\ldots,v_m\in\mathcal H$ consist of $m$ diagnostic directions, and set $V:=\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}$. Satisfying every criterion means $\langle v_i,\delta_t\rangle_{\mathcal H}=0$ for all $i=1,\ldots,m$ (equivalently $\delta_t\perp V$).

Then, satisfying these criteria cannot rule out a non-converged chain: for any such finite checklist, an ergodic chain targeting $\pi$ can satisfy, from a suitable initialization and at every finite time $t$,
\begin{equation}
\delta_t\perp V\quad\text{and}\quad\delta_t\ne0\quad\text{(hence $\pi_t\ne\pi$)},
\label{eq:passing-without-convergence}
\end{equation}
where an explicit monitor to detect this full discrepancy is the MMD witness $v_{m+1}:=\delta_t/\|\delta_t\|_{\mathcal H}$, satisfying
\begin{equation}
\langle v_{m+1},\delta_t\rangle_{\mathcal H}
=\|\delta_t\|_{\mathcal H}=\operatorname{MMD}(\pi_t,\pi)>0.
\label{eq:unmonitored-witness}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Moving $\mu_{\pi_t}$ away from $\mu_\pi$ in a direction orthogonal to $V$ leaves every monitored projection unchanged. Thus both a converged $\pi_t$ ($\delta_t=0$) and a non-converged $\pi_t$ (where $\delta_t\ne0$ and $\delta_t\perp V$) give the same zero readings for the diagnostics. The checklist therefore cannot distinguish a converged chain from a non-converged one. Appendix~\ref{app:qualitative} constructs an ergodic chain realizing the latter case at every finite time. Normalizing $\delta_t$ gives the MMD witness.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorempart-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:quantitative}
Under \textbf{(A1)},
\begin{equation}
\inf_{\dim V\le m}\ \sup_{\delta\in\mathcal B_r(R)}
\|P_{V^\perp}\delta\|_{\mathcal H}=R\lambda_{m+1}^r,
\label{eq:width}
\end{equation}
attained by the $m$ optimal monitors $e_1,\ldots,e_m$, with span $V_m^\star$. The value is unchanged if the supremum is restricted to $\delta\in V^\perp$, so this worst case remains even when all monitors are satisfied.
<!-- end theorempart-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Monitoring the first $m$ eigendirections removes the $m$ longest axes of the ellipsoid, leaving a residual of at most the next longest semi-axis, $R\lambda_{m+1}^r$. By pigeonhole, any $m$-dimensional subspace leaves a direction in the span of the first $m+1$ eigenvectors unmonitored. The ellipsoid extends at least $R\lambda_{m+1}^r$ along the unmonitored direction, giving the matching lower bound (Appendix~\ref{app:quantitative}).
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorempart-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:quantitative-rate}
Under \textbf{(A1)} and \textbf{(A2)}, the optimal residual in~\eqref{eq:width} satisfies
\[
R\lambda_{m+1}^r=\Theta(Rm^{-\alpha r}).
\]
<!-- end theorempart-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:dynamic-width}
For the ellipsoid $\mathcal B^{(t)}(R_{\mathrm{init}})$, let $d_m(t)$ be the worst discrepancy that can remain undetected at time $t$ when the best $m$ monitors are satisfied:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
d_m(t)&:=\inf_{\dim V\le m}\ \sup_{\substack{\delta\in\mathcal B^{(t)}(R_{\mathrm{init}})\\\delta\perp V}}\|\delta\|_{\mathcal H}\\
&=R_{\mathrm{init}}\sqrt{\lambda_{m+1,t}}.
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:dynamic-width}
\end{equation}
The optimal monitor span $V_m^\star(t)$ consists of the leading $m$ eigenvectors of $\Sigma_t$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:slow-optimality}
For a reversible sampler satisfying \textbf{(A3)} and \textbf{(A4)}, for all sufficiently large $t$,
\begin{equation}
\sup_{\substack{\delta\in\mathcal B^{(t)}(R_{\mathrm{init}})\\\delta\perp W_m}}\|\delta\|_{\mathcal H}
\le(1+\varepsilon_t)d_m(t),\qquad \varepsilon_t\to0.
\label{eq:slow-optimality}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By \textbf{(A4)}, omitted components shrink relative to the selected modes at rate $(a/b)^t$. The leading eigendirections of $\Sigma_t$ therefore approach $W_m$, whose worst-case residual is at most $1+o(1)$ times the optimum $d_m(t)$ in Proposition~\ref{thm:dynamic-width} (Appendix~\ref{app:slow-optimality}).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:approximate-monitors}
For $\delta_t\in\mathcal B_r(R)$ and $\theta<\pi/2$,
\begin{equation}
\delta_t\perp W\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\|\delta_t\|_{\mathcal H}\le R\lambda_{m+1}^r\sec\theta.
\label{eq:approximate-monitors}
\end{equation}
For $\mathcal B^{(t)}(R_{\mathrm{init}})$, replace $R\lambda_{m+1}^r$ by $d_m(t)$ and measure the angle to $V_m^\star(t)$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:anytime}
Suppose both component bounds hold simultaneously at every inspection time with probability at least $1-\beta$. Then, on the same event, at every inspection time,
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{MMD}(\pi_t,\pi)
\le\sqrt{M_t^2+U_t^2}.
\label{eq:anytime-residual}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Pythagoras gives $\|\delta_t\|^2=\|P_{V_t}\delta_t\|^2+\|P_{V_t^\perp}\delta_t\|^2$. Substitute the two bounds (Appendix~\ref{app:combined-bound}).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:reliability}
For this ellipsoid, the worst-case bias remaining after the best $m$ diagnostics are satisfied is
\begin{equation}
d_{b,n,m}=R_{\mathrm{init}}\sqrt{\lambda_{m+1,b,n}}.
\label{eq:average-width}
\end{equation}
For the chosen kernel $k$, let $\sigma_k^2=\|\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}>0$ be the largest target variance of a unit-norm RKHS function.

Assume each checklist can miss a bias of this size for some valid initialization under \textbf{(A3)}. The checklist then cannot guarantee mean-squared error below $d_{b,n,m}^2$ across all allowed initializations and unit-norm functions. Expressed as the accuracy of $N_{\mathrm{cert}}$ independent target draws, this gives
\begin{equation}
N_{\mathrm{cert}}\le\frac{\sigma_k^2}{d_{b,n,m}^2},
\qquad d_{b,n,m}>0.
\label{eq:certifiable-ess}
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Section~3's ellipsoid argument gives~\eqref{eq:average-width}. A hidden bias of size $d_{b,n,m}$ gives mean-squared error at least $d_{b,n,m}^2$ for its unit witness. In comparison, an average of $N$ independent target draws is unbiased and has variance $\operatorname{Var}_\pi(f(X))/N$. Its worst-case mean-squared error is therefore $\sigma_k^2/N$. Matching that accuracy requires $d_{b,n,m}^2\le\sigma_k^2/N_{\mathrm{cert}}$. Appendix~\ref{app:reliability} gives conditions for realizing the hidden bias with a valid initial law.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:lp-source}
If $K<\infty$ and $h\in L^p(\pi)$ for $1<p\le2$, then
\[
\mu_Q-\mu_\pi=\Sigma^{1-1/p}u,
\qquad \|u\|\le K^{2/p-1}\|h\|_p.
\]
Thus \textbf{(A1)} holds with $r=1-1/p$. For $p=2$, the radius is $\|h\|_2=\sqrt{\chi^2(Q\|\pi)}$, the square root of the chi-square divergence \citep{sason2016fdivergence}.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For $p=2$, polar decomposition gives $B=\Sigma^{1/2}U$ with $\|U\|\le1$. For $1<p<2$, let $P_N$ project onto the first $N$ positive covariance eigendirections and consider $T_z=\Sigma^{-z/2}P_NB$ on $0\le\operatorname{Re}z\le1$. Its boundary norms satisfy
\[
\|T_{iy}\|_{L^1\to\mathcal H}\le K,
\qquad
\|T_{1+iy}\|_{L^2\to\mathcal H}\le1.
\]
Complex interpolation at $\theta=2-2/p$ yields
\[
\|\Sigma^{-(1-1/p)}P_NBh\|
\le K^{2/p-1}\|h\|_p
\]
uniformly in $N$ \citep{stein1956interpolation}. Taking the limit of the squared spectral norms gives the required $u$. No component of $Bh$ lies in $\ker\Sigma$: a centered feature in such a direction vanishes $\pi$-almost surely and hence $Q$-almost surely.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For $\delta\perp W$, the principal-angle identity gives $\|P_V\delta\|\le\sin\theta\|\delta\|$. Hence
\[
\cos\theta\|\delta\|
\le\|P_{V^\perp}\delta\|
\le d_m,
\]
where the last inequality is the source-class bound. Dividing by $\cos\theta$ proves the result.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:nonlinear-moments}
Let $c_1,\ldots,c_q\in L^1(\pi)$, and suppose $\pi$ admits $q+2$ disjoint sets of positive probability. For diagnostics
\[
D_\ell(P)=F_\ell\bigl(\mathbb E_P[c_1],\ldots,\mathbb E_P[c_q]\bigr),
\]
with each $F_\ell$ defined at the target moment vector, there is an ergodic chain targeting $\pi$ such that every $D_\ell(\pi_t)=D_\ell(\pi)$ at every finite time, while $\pi_t\ne\pi$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The nullspace construction in Appendix~\ref{app:qualitative}, applied to $1,c_1,\ldots,c_q$, gives a bounded nonzero $h$ satisfying $\mathbb E_\pi h=0$ and $\mathbb E_\pi[h c_j]=0$ for every $j$. Scale it so that $\|h\|_\infty<1$. Then $dQ=(1+h)d\pi$ is a probability law with the same moments as $\pi$. The refresh kernel from that appendix gives $\pi_t-\pi=(1-\rho)^t(Q-\pi)$, so those moments, and hence every diagnostic $D_\ell$, retain their target values at every finite time.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:path-features}
If $\pi$ admits $p+2$ disjoint positive-probability sets, there is an initial law $\pi_0\ne\pi$ with bounded positive density relative to $\pi$ that matches all $p$ stationary path expectations. If $\mathcal P^*$ is injective on $L^2_0(\pi)$, then $\pi_t\ne\pi$ at every finite time.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Apply Appendix~\ref{app:qualitative}'s construction to $1,g_1,\ldots,g_p$. It gives a nonzero $h_0$ with $\|h_0\|_\infty<1$ orthogonal to every constraint. The time-$t$ density error is $(\mathcal P^*)^t h_0$, which remains nonzero under injectivity. The refresh kernel satisfies this condition because $\mathcal P^*=(1-\rho)I$ on mean-zero functions.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Independence gives $\mathbb E\|\widehat\mu_t-\mu_{\pi_t}\|^2\le\kappa^2/J$, so the expected norm is at most $\kappa/\sqrt J$. Replacing one observation changes that norm by at most $2\kappa/J$. The bounded-differences inequality gives the radius in~\eqref{eq:replica-radius} with failure probability $\beta_\mu w_t$. Sum these probabilities over inspection times.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
If $R_{\mathrm{init}}K_{m+1}\le1$, every diagnostic span of dimension at most $m$ admits an initial probability law satisfying \textbf{(A3)} whose retained-average discrepancy is orthogonal to that span and has norm $d_{b,n,m}$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
For a diagnostic span $V$, choose a unit vector $w=\sum_{j=1}^{m+1}w_ju_j$ orthogonal to $V$, and set
\[
h=R_{\mathrm{init}}s_{m+1}
\sum_{j=1}^{m+1}\frac{w_j}{s_j}a_j.
\]
Then $\mathbb E_\pi h=0$, $\|h\|_2\le R_{\mathrm{init}}$, and $\|h\|_\infty\le R_{\mathrm{init}}K_{m+1}\le1$. Thus $d\pi_0=(1+h)d\pi$ is a probability law satisfying \textbf{(A3)}. Its retained-average discrepancy is
\[
A_{b,n}h=R_{\mathrm{init}}s_{m+1}w=d_{b,n,m}w,
\]
which satisfies every diagnostic in $V$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
